cards.front: Foundation model vs LLM (in this book)?
cards.back: LLM: large language model. Foundation model: broader—may be multimodal or general-purpose; adapted via prompting, RAG, or finetuning for many downstream tasks.
Autoregressive predicts the next token from prior tokens (standard for text generation). Masked (e.g. BERT) uses bidirectional context—common for non-generative tasks.

cards.front: Three main ways to adapt a foundation model?
cards.back: Prompt engineering (no weight change), RAG (external context), finetuning (continued training on your data/task).
Infrastructure → model development (pre-training, post-training, data, inference) → application development (product, eval, prompts, UI).

cards.front: How does AI engineering workflow differ from classical ML?
cards.back: Often product-first: ship with a shared foundation model, then add specialized data/models only if the product proves value—inverted from bespoke-model-first ML.
Tasks needing external tools, planning, and multi-step actions—not just text in/out.

questions.prompt: A foundation model is best described as:
choices: A model trained only on labeled tabular data
A large pretrained model adaptable to many tasks via prompting, RAG, or finetuning
questions.explanation: Chapter 1 frames FMs as the shared base; differentiation moves to the application layer.

questions.prompt: For open-ended text generation today, the book defaults to:
questions.explanation: Unless stated otherwise, “language model” means autoregressive generation.

questions.prompt: Application-layer differentiation most often comes from:
choices: Training a new foundation model from scratch
Evaluation, prompts/context, and product UX on shared models
questions.explanation: With shared base models, product and eval—not pre-training—are the moat for most teams.

choices: Only which API key to use
Use-case fit, human/AI roles, metrics, and defensibility
Only the font in the UI
questions.explanation: Chapter 1 stresses use-case evaluation, expectations, and moats—not jumping to prompts.

questions.prompt: AI engineering vs traditional MLOps differs mainly because:
choices: FMs shift effort toward adaptation, eval, and product on shared models
questions.explanation: The discipline spans the stack but emphasizes adaptation and evaluation over bespoke training for most apps.
